newsitem.title: USA: USDA - weak demand from Japan hurts US pork exports.
newsitem.headline: USDA - weak demand from Japan hurts US pork exports.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department revised downward its forecast for U.S. pork exports largely due to weaker demand from Japan than previously expected, a department official said Thursday.

"Exports are just not performing like we thought they were going to," said James Nix, chairperson of USDA's World Agricultural Outlook Board committee on meat. "Demand in Japan seems weak and we're just not getting the business we expected."

Earlier, in a monthly report, USDA shaved its forecast for 1997 U.S. pork exports to 1.250 billion lbs from 1.355 billion lbs seen in May. It also lowered its estimate for 1998 pork exports to 1.465 billion lbs from 1.580 billion lbs.
CME hog and pork belly futures tumbled on the news.

Nix said the department had expected more of a pick-up in U.S. pork exports due to an outbreak of hog disease in Taiwan which has blocked exports from Taiwan for the foreseeable future. Japan was the largest export market for Taiwan pork.
"There's still a lot of increase in there but it's not coming on as strong as we what we first thought here that it might," he said.
Nix said USDA also had expected to see more sales by now because Japan's pork import tariff expires at the end of June.
He noted that food safety concerns in Japan have hurt beef and pork demand.
Nix said despite the downward revision, exports were still strong. "Even though its down from where we had it, it's still a sizeable increase in exports from year to year."
U.S. pork exports in 1996 totalled 951 million lbs.
